A useful analogy is the surface of an inflating balloon: as it expands, every point on the surface moves away from every other point, but there is no centre *on the surface*. The balloon’s centre exists only in the higher-dimensional space of the analogy, not within the two-dimensional surface.

Likewise, in our three-dimensional universe, galaxies recede from one another because space between them expands. Any observer in any galaxy would see distant galaxies moving away in roughly the same pattern, and could mistakenly conclude they were at the centre.

There is a “centre of the observable universe”: it is us, because the observable universe is simply the region whose light has had time to reach us. An observer elsewhere would have a different observable universe centered on them.

The universe could be infinite, in which case it has no centre by definition. Or it could be finite but curved and unbounded—somewhat like the balloon surface—where it may still have no internal central point. Measurements of the cosmic microwave background and galaxy distribution are consistent with a universe that is homogeneous and has no preferred central location on large scales.

An analogy: imagine dots painted on an expanding balloon surface. Rewind the balloon’s expansion and all the dots get closer together. At the earliest stage the surface is tiny, but no dot on the surface is the place the expansion started. Every dot can reasonably say, “the expansion happened here too.”

So there may have been an extremely small early universe, but not a special location *within the universe* where the Big Bang happened. Every location in today’s universe traces back to that early state.

Not necessarily. A centre of mass is well-defined only when certain conditions hold.

In ordinary physics, you calculate it by averaging the positions of all the mass:

\[
\mathbf r_{\rm CM}=\frac{\sum m_i\mathbf r_i}{\sum m_i}.
\]

That assumes there is a meaningful shared coordinate system in which all the objects have positions, and that the total mass and the average are finite and well-defined.

For the whole universe, those assumptions may fail:

- **If the universe is infinite and roughly uniform**, it contains infinitely much matter in every direction. There is no finite “average position” of all its mass, so no global centre of mass.
- **If space is finite but curved and has no boundary**, such as the three-dimensional analogue of a sphere’s surface, there need not be a central point *in the space itself*. A sphere’s surface has mass and is finite, but no point on the surface is its centre of mass. You can speak of a centre only by imagining the surface embedded in a higher-dimensional outside space.
- **In general relativity**, mass-energy and spacetime geometry are linked, and a universal, coordinate-independent centre of mass is not generally defined for an expanding entire universe the way it is for a baseball or solar system.

There *are* centres of mass for local, bounded systems: Earth, the Solar System, the Milky Way, galaxy clusters, and so on. Those are physical objects with identifiable boundaries and finite mass.

You can also define a centre of mass for the **observable universe**, after choosing a coordinate system and specifying which matter is included. But that would be a property of our observable patch, not proof of a unique centre of the whole universe or the location of the Big Bang. Another distant observer’s observable patch would be centered differently.

So “everything physical has a centre of mass” is a good approximation for everyday finite objects in ordinary space—not a rule that automatically applies to spacetime as a whole.
